headline: Animated Gaussian Splats Arrive as Nvidia's AI Rendering Draws Fire
lede: A small Chinese startup walked away from SIGGRAPH 2025's most prestigious live-demonstration prize with software that converts ordinary video footage into navigable four-dimensional scenes. In the same season, Nvidia's flagship AI rendering suite earned the label “AI slop” from its own chief executive — a collision of timing that sharpens a genuine debate about what machine learning is actually doing to computer graphics.
body:
The company is **4DV.ai** (the tweet cites a slightly transposed URL, `4vd.ai`, which appears to be a typo), a Chinese startup whose *InfiniteStudio* system won Best in Show at *Real-Time Live!* — SIGGRAPH's live-demonstration competition — in 2025. The product converts standard multi-camera video footage into a navigable four-dimensional scene: three spatial dimensions plus time, reconstructable from any viewpoint in a browser via *WebXR*, without special software installation. The underlying technology is **4D Gaussian splatting**, a pipeline that processes a full second of production footage thirty times faster than competing systems, according to the company, and compresses the result to between 80 and 120 Mbps for distribution to Apple Vision Pro (AAPL), Meta (META) Quest, and PC headsets.

*3D Gaussian splatting* (3DGS), the technique’s foundation, was introduced in a paper by Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, and Drettakis that won SIGGRAPH’s Best Paper prize in 2023. Where earlier *neural radiance field* (NeRF) approaches require a neural network to evaluate every screen pixel during rendering — limiting throughput to single-digit frame rates — 3DGS represents a scene as millions of semi-transparent ellipsoidal blobs, each carrying position, orientation, colour, and opacity values. Rendering projects these blobs onto the image plane via standard GPU *rasterization*, achieving over 100 frames per second on consumer hardware. Adding a time axis requires a *deformation field*: a learned function that repositions each Gaussian across frames without storing a separate point cloud per timestep. By 2024, academic teams were demonstrating 82-fps dynamic reconstructions on a consumer GPU with training runs under thirty minutes.

The contrast the tweet draws is with Nvidia’s (NVDA) *DLSS* — *Deep Learning Super Sampling* — which launched in 2018 with a legitimate premise: render internally at lower resolution, then use AI to reconstruct a sharper image, giving mid-range hardware performance above its class. DLSS 4 (January 2025) expanded that mission to *Multi Frame Generation*, which synthesises three to five wholly artificial frames for every real rendered frame. Most of what appears on screen in heavily frame-generated footage was never computed from game geometry at all. Hardware reviewers documented specific artefacts: *ghosting*, where synthetic frames misplace fast-moving objects; smearing of thin geometry such as barbed wire and distant architecture; and latency climbing above 100 milliseconds in demanding scenarios.

DLSS 5 (March 2026) crossed a different line. Where prior versions altered pixels after rendering, DLSS 5 applies *neural rendering* at the geometry level — altering lighting, textures, and character features during the rendering pass itself. Demonstrations showed a character from *Resident Evil: Requiem* with reshaped facial geometry reflecting the AI model’s aesthetic preferences rather than the developer’s design intent. Senior game artists described the result as disrespectful to intentional art direction; the YouTube showcase drew roughly 84 percent dislikes. Nvidia’s chief executive initially called the critics “completely wrong”; within days, on the Lex Fridman podcast, he reversed course: “I don’t love AI slop myself… all of the AI generated content increasingly looks similar, and they’re all beautiful, and so I’m empathetic towards what they’re thinking.”

The substantive distinction is philosophical. 4DV.ai’s pipeline starts with cameras and uses machine learning to reconstruct geometry that was genuinely there. DLSS 5 starts with a rendered frame and generates detail that was not. One discipline tries to capture the world more faithfully; the other optimises toward a more aesthetically generic substitute for it. That **AI slop** — content homogenised toward a learned visual ideal — earned its name from Nvidia’s own chief executive suggests the criticism has landed somewhere the company cannot easily dismiss.

concepts.definition: An extension of 3D Gaussian splatting that adds a time dimension, allowing a scene to be reconstructed from video footage as an animated, navigable 3D environment. A deformation field repositions each Gaussian blob across frames so the system stores motion rather than a separate point cloud per timestep.

A real-time rendering technique introduced at SIGGRAPH 2023 that represents a scene as millions of semi-transparent 3D blobs (Gaussians), each with position, orientation, colour, and opacity. Rendered via standard GPU rasterization, it achieves over 100 fps novel-view synthesis on consumer hardware — far faster than NeRF, which requires neural-network inference per pixel.

A technique for synthesising novel views of a scene by training a neural network on a set of photographs. The network is queried for every screen pixel during rendering, which produces high visual quality but is far too slow for real-time use — typically under 10 fps even on powerful hardware.

The dominant real-time graphics pipeline: 3D geometry is projected onto a 2D image plane and converted to pixels using a depth buffer. Modern GPUs are heavily optimised for this process. Both 3DGS and polygon-based game engines exploit rasterization, which is why 3DGS achieves real-time speed where NeRF cannot.

In 4D Gaussian splatting, a learned function that maps each Gaussian blob from a canonical resting configuration to a new position, orientation, and scale at a given moment in time. This allows a dynamic scene to be stored as one canonical Gaussian cloud plus a compact motion model, rather than a full snapshot per frame.

A browser API standard that enables virtual and augmented reality experiences on the web without native app installation. 4DV.ai uses WebXR to deliver navigable volumetric video scenes to headsets including Apple Vision Pro, Meta Quest, and PC VR rigs through a standard browser session.

Nvidia’s suite of AI-driven graphics enhancement technologies. Originally designed to upscale a lower-resolution rendered image to fill a higher-resolution display, it has expanded to include frame generation (synthesising artificial frames between real ones) and, in its fifth version, neural rendering that alters geometry-level detail.

A component of DLSS 4 and later that generates three to five synthetic frames for every real rendered frame using optical flow and AI interpolation. Boosts displayed frame rates but introduces latency, artefacts on thin geometry, and UI duplication errors, because most displayed frames contain no information actually computed from game geometry.

A broad term for using neural networks to produce or modify images within the rendering pipeline. In DLSS 5 specifically, it refers to a generative model applied at the geometry level that alters lighting, textures, and surface detail — in contrast to post-process upscaling, which operates on an already-rendered 2D frame.

A visual artefact in frame-generated footage where a faint duplicate or echo of a fast-moving object appears in the wrong position because the AI predicted its trajectory incorrectly. In ‘reverse ghosting’ the echo appears on the leading edge of motion rather than the trailing edge, because the model has over-anticipated the object’s path.

Informal term for AI-generated content that is aesthetically over-smoothed, generic, or homogenised — recognisably the output of a model optimised for broad appeal rather than specific artistic intent. In the graphics context it refers to rendered images or frames that look AI-made: overly sharp, beauty-standardised, and detached from the artist’s original vision.

fact_check: The tweet links to '4vd.ai', but the company's live domain appears to be '4dv.ai' — the 'd' and 'v' are transposed. The URL '4vd.ai' returned a connection error at the time of research. This is almost certainly a typo in the original post rather than a deliberate distinction.
